 Peruvian grape harvest races ahead of rainy season as growers push for early finish
 A brief spell of rainfall in northern Peru has raised some concerns in the sector, though the region's sandy soils are expected to drain quickly. Meanwhile, high temperatures have accelerated grape ripening, and growers are pushing to complete the harvest before the rainy season sets in.
 Alonso Puga, of Proserla, says that the rain was an isolated incident and, for now, sees no signs of the arrival of El Niño, so he urged the sector to stay calm.
 © Proserla 
 "It rained in Piura, and not in our area, in Lambayeque or Jayanca. And it only rained for one day, no more," says Puga. "Today it's no longer raining." He believes that the rainy season has not yet begun.
 According to Puga, the rainfall is the result of the transfer rains from the mountain range typical of this time of year, not El Niño. "I don't believe they are linked to the phenomenon," he says, adding that El Niño typically becomes active in northern Peru between late December and April, with peak intensity between January and March.
 On the potential impact on crops, Puga is cautious, as he is not in the affected area, but he remains confident that damage will be limited, given the nature of the soil. "The soils in Piura are loose, so they will surely drain without any problems. I don't think the impact will be that severe, and let's hope that's the case," he says.
 Since the soils are sandy, sunshine should help bring the situation back to normal fairly quickly. "I know the sun will come out and everyone will feel more at ease," he says.
 © Proserla 
 Harvesting ahead of the rainy season 
For the grape campaign, the company's strategy is to speed up picking and "get it delivered as fast as possible," says Puga. The high temperatures of recent weeks have helped, causing varieties to ripen earlier than usual.
 The goal is to complete the harvest before the period when El Niño typically becomes active. "We're trying to harvest as quickly as possible to be done with the season in time," he says. The plan is to finish before the end of December. "By mid-December we should already be done," says Puga.
